verdicts.framing_note: The claim's "manual approval remains close to universal" paraphrases the source's "almost every change still needs manual approval". The 63% figure and its subject (trust in agents making production changes) match the source exactly.

verdicts.text: In Pulumi's 2026 survey, the share of teams expecting agents to generate half or more of their infrastructure code rises from 45% today to 52% within six months.
verdicts.evidence: The cited page returned HTTP 200 and is titled "State of Agentic Infrastructure 2026 | Pulumi", so the survey exists. But the pre-fetched body cuts off in the site navigation, before any survey results, so the 45% and 52% figures and the "within six months" framing could not be checked.
verdicts.framing_note: The supporting passage is not in the fetched content, so no framing check was possible. Also check whether the source measures "teams" or "respondents", and whether it says "expect" or "plan".

verdicts.text: Pulumi's blog post 'The Agentic Infrastructure Era' argues AIOps is headed toward a supervised agentic operating model rather than faster dashboards and alerting alone.
verdicts.evidence: The claim attributes an argument to the Pulumi blog post 'The Agentic Infrastructure Era', but the pre-fetched URL is the Neo product page, not that post. The fetched body is only navigation text ("Pulumi Neo - Your AI Infrastructure Agent ... Meet Neo, our AI-powered infrastructure engineering agent") and says nothing about AIOps or a supervised agentic operating model.
verdicts.framing_note: Target mismatch: the claim names a blog post, but the link points to the Neo product page. Check the post under content/blog/ in the repo instead.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The link may be wrong: the text names a blog post but links to /product/neo/.

verdicts.text: According to Mordor Intelligence, the global Kubernetes market is projected to reach USD 8.41 billion by 2031, a 21.85% CAGR.
verdicts.evidence: The cited Mordor Intelligence page returned HTTP 403 Forbidden with an empty body, so I could not quote any passage to confirm the USD 8.41 billion by 2031 figure or the 21.85% CAGR. A 403 usually means the site blocked the bot, not that the link is dead, so I'm not calling this a broken citation.
verdicts.framing_note: Couldn't run the framing check: the page returned 403 and no source text was available.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Mordor updates its projections every year, so the 2031 end year and the 21.85% CAGR may have been swapped into a post titled '2024 and beyond'. Worth a web check to see if they match the current report.

verdicts.text: The CNCF's Q3 2025 State of Cloud Native Development report says 30% of backend developers now use Kubernetes directly, down from a peak of 36% in Q3 2023.
verdicts.evidence: The cited PDF returned HTTP 200, but the pre-fetched body is compressed binary PDF streams with no readable text. I couldn't find or quote any passage about 30% of backend developers using Kubernetes or a 36% peak in Q3 2023.
verdicts.framing_note: The framing check couldn't be run because the PDF text wasn't extracted. When re-checking, make sure "use Kubernetes directly" and "backend developers" match the report's own wording and population.

verdicts.text: Inference workloads powered by LLMs and GPUs now require low-latency execution closer to the user, pushing organizations to build orchestration layers that schedule AI pipelines across edge and core clusters, often using Kubernetes as the common control plane.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Several 2025–2026 industry and research sources describe the same trend. An arXiv paper says LLM services "increasingly operate on edge infrastructure, enabling low-latency and privacy-preserving AI services", and Rafay says Kubernetes "connects compute resources across edge and datacenter environments" for AI inference. Other sources describe GPU-aware Kubernetes orchestration layers that span edge and cloud clusters.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is a broad, uncited trend claim. The sources show the pattern is growing, not that all LLM inference "now requires" running at the edge. Most LLM inference still runs centrally in the cloud.

verdicts.text: [Kubernetes is also evolving in response to AI demands](https://www.pulumi.com/blog/beyond-yaml-kubernetes-2026-automation-era/#the-2026-convergence-of-ai-platforms-and-policy-in-kubernetes), a shift Pulumi covers in more depth in its [comparison of Kubernetes IaC tools](https://www.pulumi.com/blog/
verdicts.evidence: The cited URL returned HTTP 200 with the title "Beyond YAML in Kubernetes: The 2026 Automation Era | Pulumi Blog". The fetched body was cut off after the site navigation, so I couldn't read or quote the #the-2026-convergence-of-ai-platforms-and-policy-in-kubernetes section. The anchor name fits the claim that "Kubernetes is also evolving in response to AI demands", but that alone doesn't confirm it.
verdicts.framing_note: The anchor name ('convergence of AI platforms and policy in Kubernetes') matches the link text ('Kubernetes is evolving in response to AI demands'), but the section text wasn't in the fetched content.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A blog post titled '2024 and beyond' links to a post about 2026. That's probably fine for a refreshed post, but worth a look.

verdicts.text: Kubernetes is evolving to support AI through GPU-aware scheduling and more advanced workload orchestration.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) became GA in 1.34 and brings attribute-aware GPU scheduling. Sources describe it as "the foundation for more advanced scheduling patterns" for AI workloads, alongside Kueue and KAI Scheduler, which handle AI orchestration.
verdicts.framing_note: General trend claim with no cited source. Several independent sources back it, but they are third-party blogs, not the official kubernetes.io release notes, so confidence is medium.

verdicts.text: According to Gartner, 63% of organizations are currently piloting, deploying or beginning to use AI code assistants (figure from a 2024 Gartner press release, presented as current).
verdicts.evidence: The Gartner press release from April 11, 2024 says: "Sixty-three percent of organizations are currently piloting, deploying or have already deployed AI code assistants, according to a Gartner survey of 598 global respondents in the third quarter of 2023." The 63% figure and the attribution to Gartner are correct. However, the claim changes "have already deployed" to "beginning to use," and it presents a Q3 2023 survey result as current without giving the date.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted — the source says 'piloting, deploying or have already deployed' but the claim says 'piloting, deploying or beginning to use'. The claim also drops the survey date (Q3 2023) while still presenting the figure as 'currently'.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The survey data is from Q3 2023 but is called 'current' in a post that is still live in 2026. Consider adding the date.

verdicts.text: The Model Context Protocol had a July 2026 revision, described by its maintainers as the largest revision of the protocol to date.
verdicts.evidence: The page confirms that the July 2026 revision exists: "Today, we're officially pushing the release button on the next version of the MCP specification, 2026-07-28". The fetched text is cut off, though, and the part we have never calls it the "largest revision" of the protocol, so that attribution is unconfirmed.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim's date is confirmed. The superlative "largest revision of the protocol to date" is credited to the maintainers, but the fetched text doesn't contain it. The post calls the stateless core "the highlight of this release", not the largest revision.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This superlative quote may be the writer's own wording presented as the maintainers'. Check the full post for "largest".

verdicts.text: The July 2026 MCP revision is part of what makes direct action by AI assistants on infrastructure practical.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The MCP 2026-07-28 revision is real. It shipped on July 28, 2026, and the official MCP blog says it brings "a stateless protocol core, Multi Round-Trip Requests, header-based routing, cacheable list results, authorization hardening". The official announcement and industry coverage describe this as production and enterprise maturation of the protocol AI agents use to call tools. That supports the editorial point that the revision helps make direct AI action on infrastructure practical.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names no source. The fact it rests on (a July 2026 MCP revision exists) is confirmed. The part about it enabling direct action is the author's editorial reading, and the official changelog and coverage are consistent with it.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is a soft causal/editorial claim. Only the existence and scope of the revision can be checked. Also note that this blog post's slug says "2024" but the text references July 2026 events.

verdicts.text: Mirantis's Lens launched a built-in MCP server connecting AI coding assistants to Kubernetes.
verdicts.evidence: The cited Mirantis press page (HTTP 200) is titled "Lens Launches Built-In MCP Server | Mirantis". It is filed under Mirantis company news, and its URL slug reads "lens-launches-built-in-mcp-server-connecting-ai-coding-assistants-to-kubernetes". The pre-fetched body cuts off before the article text, so I could only confirm the title and slug, not the full article.
verdicts.framing_note: The page title and slug say the same thing as the claim. Calling Lens "Mirantis's" matches the page being in Mirantis's own press center.

verdicts.text: As enterprise adoption of AI assistants increases, expectations are rising: they must not only generate code but also understand the state of infrastructure, configurations, and security posture. That means being able to answer questions about environments, surface misconfigurations, or act directly
verdicts.evidence: The cited page loaded (HTTP 200), but it is the announcement of the MCP 2026-07-28 specification ("bringing a stateless protocol core, Multi Round-Trip Requests, header-based routing..."). Nothing in the fetched text covers enterprise adoption of AI assistants or rising expectations that they understand infrastructure state and security posture. The only growth figure is about SDK downloads.
verdicts.framing_note: The source is a protocol spec release post, not a survey of enterprise AI-assistant adoption or expectations. The claim is also qualitative and has no numeric anchor, despite being typed "numerical".
verdicts.intuition_flag: A post about "2024 and beyond" trends cites a July 2026 MCP spec post for a general claim about enterprise adoption. The citation may be misplaced, or it may belong to a nearby sentence about MCP.

verdicts.text: AWS shipped a general-availability MCP server for its Agent Toolkit.
verdicts.evidence: The cited AWS What's New page (HTTP 200) is titled "The AWS MCP Server is now generally available", which confirms the GA MCP server. The truncated body doesn't show the announcement text that ties it to the Agent Toolkit. The only link in what was fetched is a nav item: "Give AI coding agents up-to-date docs and AWS resource access", eyebrow "Agent Toolkit".
verdicts.framing_note: The source title confirms 'AWS MCP Server is now generally available'. The 'for its Agent Toolkit' part is only suggested by the site nav, not confirmed by the announcement body, which was truncated.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Agent Skills teach AI coding tools such as Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI to reason about Pulumi projects, reducing hallucination and improving outputs.
verdicts.evidence: The cited post backs the tool list and the "teaches" part: "packaged expertise that teaches any AI coding assistant how to work with Pulumi the way an experienced practitioner would" and "They work across multiple AI coding platforms including Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, VS Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI." A grep of the source file found no mention of hallucination. The post describes a different problem: code that "works but misses the mark on patterns that matter."
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the claim turns "code that works but misses the mark on patterns that matter" into "reducing hallucination". The source never promises a hallucination benefit.

verdicts.text: Pulumi released Pulumi Agent Skills, a collection of infrastructure expertise packaged for use in AI coding assistants, described as one of the newest developments.
verdicts.evidence: The cited Pulumi blog post (dated 2026-01-29) says: "That is why we are releasing Pulumi Agent Skills, a collection of packaged expertise that teaches any AI coding assistant how to work with Pulumi the way an experienced practitioner would." That backs up both the release and the description. "Newest" is a recency judgment. It depends on when the reader sees it, and the source doesn't state it.
verdicts.framing_note: Source: "releasing Pulumi Agent Skills, a collection of packaged expertise" for AI coding assistants. Claim: "a collection of infrastructure expertise packaged for use in AI coding assistants."
verdicts.intuition_flag: "One of the newest developments" points to a January 2026 release. The paragraph right before it cites a July 2026 MCP revision and a May 2026 AWS release, so calling it one of the newest could go stale.

verdicts.text: Pulumi provides a Remote MCP Server that gives AI assistants infrastructure access, and Pulumi Neo executes actions with previews, policies, and orchestration.
verdicts.evidence: The cited announcement says the Remote MCP Server lets AI assistants "instantly access your Pulumi Cloud infrastructure, search resources across stacks, and delegate complex automation tasks to Pulumi Neo." The Neo docs say Neo "Runs previews before anything lands… surface policy violations" and adds "policy guardrails, human-in-the-loop approvals," and the blog lists Neo's "Multi-step planning", which covers the orchestration part.
verdicts.framing_note: The cited blog supports the MCP half of the claim word for word. The previews and policy wording comes from the Neo docs page rather than the cited post.

verdicts.text: Modern IaC, unified governance, reusable components, and policy frameworks are all core capabilities of the Pulumi Cloud platform.
verdicts.evidence: Other product docs in the repo back up all four capabilities. The pricing page counts "[component resources](/docs/iac/concepts/components) which are groupings of resources" and mentions "policy execution" in Discovery and "RBAC for advanced policy controls." Pulumi's docs also cover IaC (/docs/iac/), Pulumi Policies (/docs/insights/policy/) and Insights + governance (/product/insights-governance/).
verdicts.source: repo:content/pricing/_index.md L52, L99, L134; Pulumi docs/product paths /docs/iac/, /docs/insights/policy/, /product/insights-governance/
verdicts.framing_note: Broad marketing summary; small point: IaC and components are open-source Pulumi IaC features that Pulumi Cloud builds on, not features only Pulumi Cloud has.
